title: Numbers from India
hookLine: the Indian numerals, with zero, travel west through Arabic books

cards: Try writing nine hundred eighteen in Roman numerals. You get a tangle of letters, and adding two of them together is a headache. Write it the usual way, a few digits in a row, and any schoolchild can add it.

The trick is in the empty places: a small circle that means nothing is here, and because it holds the place, every other digit knows what it's worth. In English those digits are often called Arabic numerals.
In the Arabic books of Baghdad, the method had another name. They called it Indian reckoning.

teach.h: A SIGN'S PLACE TELLS ITS SIZE.
teach.b: The idea came from India. Indian mathematicians wrote numbers with a small set of signs, where a sign's place in the row tells its size: ones on the far right, then tens, then hundreds.

teach.h: AN EMPTY PLACE NEEDS A MARK.
teach.b: And when a place is empty, you need a mark that says so, or the whole row slides. That mark is the one we call zero.
Scholars writing in Arabic took up this Indian way of counting and wrote books to teach it; al-Khwarizmi, from yesterday, is credited with one of them.
Later readers in Europe learned the method from those Arabic books, so in Europe the figures got an Arabic name, while the Arabic books kept calling them Indian. Both names are honest.
Each one tells you where a neighbor first met the idea.
The Arabic word for the empty place was sifr, meaning empty.
So nothing became a number: an emptiness you can write down, add, and build on. A row of digits works because some places are allowed to be empty and still be counted.
The Qur'an says that God keeps count of all things, and some Muslim readers have heard in that a reason to count carefully and honestly.
Either way, the empty place now had a mark of its own, and a long sum could be written down and checked, one place at a time.

practice: Draw one slow circle with a pen, or trace it with a finger on your palm, and look at the empty middle: it isn't nothing at all, it holds a place.

Let it stand for one empty place in your own day, a gap in the calendar or a quiet hour, counted as part of the day and not a waste. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet with God; if not, just rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Sifr, empty: the Arabic word for the empty place in a row of digits, the mark we call zero, carried west through Arabic books from India's way of counting. Today's word.
